title: Embracing Discrete Search: A Reasonable Approach to Causal Structure Learning
claim: Our method reaches near-zero structural error at a fraction of the run-time, while competing algorithms are slower, less accurate, or both.
layout: 2 side-by-side scatter plots, shared x-axis, colored diamonds mark per-method averages
description: Two side-by-side scatter plots share the x-axis, runtime in seconds from 0 to 8. The left y-axis is Structural Hamming Distance (SHD) and the right is Ancestor Adjustment Identification Distance (AID). Each method is a cloud of translucent dots, one per random instance, with a large outlined diamond at its mean. Labels sit next to each cloud. The colors are pink, red and salmon for the FLOP variants (FLOP_0, FLOP_20, FLOP_100), teal for BOSS, yellow-olive for PC, blue for GES and gray for DAGMA. The FLOP and BOSS clouds sit near zero error. FLOP_0 and FLOP_20 sit far left at low runtime, and FLOP_100 and BOSS sit near 5 seconds. PC, GES and DAGMA sit high above, with errors of 200 to 1500. The eye goes first to the lower-left corner, where the FLOP clusters are.
caption: Run-time plotted against Structural Hamming Distance (left) and Ancestor Adjustment Identification Distance (Henckel et al., 2024) (right) between the CPDAGs learned on linear ANM data and the target CPDAG corresponding to the underlying Erd˝os-Renyi generated DAG with 50 nodes, average degree 8 and 1000 samples drawn. Every point corresponds to one of 50 random instances; diamonds indicate averages. FLOP variants differ in the number of ILS restarts to escape local optima. The fraction of instances with exact CPDAG recovery is 40% for BOSS and FLOP0 and 60% for FLOP20 and FLOP100, and zero for the remaining algorithms.
abstract: We present FLOP (Fast Learning of Order and Parents), a score-based causal discovery algorithm for linear models. It pairs fast parent selection with iterative Cholesky-based score updates, cutting run-times over prior algorithms. This makes it feasible to fully embrace discrete search, enabling iterated local search with principled order initialization to find graphs with scores at or close to the global optimum. The resulting structures are highly accurate across benchmarks, with near-perfect recovery in standard settings. This performance calls for revisiting discrete search over graphs as a reasonable approach to causal discovery.
